chapters.title: Good and Bad Strategy
chapters.hook: A service-ticket printout can expose a fake strategy faster than a polished growth deck.
chapters.counterintuition: Ambition can sound decisive and still dodge the hard diagnosis when no obstacle has been named. Good strategy starts with the constraint that governs action.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one active plan and write three lines: the obstacle, the chosen response, and one action you would cut because it does not serve either one.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A plan earns the name strategy only when it names the real obstacle, chooses a response, and aligns action tightly enough that scattered effort becomes force.

breakdown.fastRead:
Rebecca sets the service-ticket printout where the laptop was supposed to sit. The repair counter has six fixes proposed, but the printout shows one fact: cracked screens are waiting nine days because parts are scattered across stores. She crosses out the marketing push, the training video, and the new sign. The problem is not energy. The problem is the shape of the work.

Good strategy starts where the real obstacle is named. It names the real obstacle before it rewards action. Bad strategy starts with ambition and then gathers projects around it.

The near-bankrupt company makes the contrast sharp. The company was close to bankruptcy, and the useful move was not a grander speech. The rescue narrowed products, channels, software work, factories, and stock toward survival in personal computers.
breakdown.deepRead:
Apple in September 1997 was not saved by louder ambition; the visible move was a hard narrowing of products, channels, software, factories, and inventory around the problem in front of it. Steve Jobs made the strategy visible by cutting the product maze down until the company could act coherently again. Desktop models went to one. Portable and handheld lines were reduced. Peripherals, retailers, software efforts, manufacturing arrangements, and inventory all faced the same pressure. That matters because the moves were not random cuts. They pointed at one diagnosis: Apple was too complicated for its condition.

A real diagnosis changes the room.

Without it, every action can plead for itself. The repair counter wants a better sign. The store manager wants training. The regional lead wants a promotion. Each suggestion can sound reasonable, which is why bad strategy survives. It lets reasonable pieces sit together without asking what problem should govern them.

Thomas sees the same pattern in a hospital discharge meeting. The nurse callback log shows that weekend patients are returning because medication instructions are being handed off twice, once by a resident and once by a rotating nurse. The room wants a new discharge checklist and a Saturday staffing grid, but the two fixes pull against each other. Thomas points at the callback log and asks which failure they are truly answering before any vote happens.

That is the hard part. A diagnosis does not merely explain. It removes cover. Once the obstacle is named, attractive actions that do not fit start to look expensive, even when their champions still sound sincere.

Good strategy is governed choice. Bad strategy is protected activity.
breakdown.fullRead:
The Microsoft $150 million investment bought Apple time, but money alone did not become the strategy. Time only mattered because the company was being narrowed into a shape that could use it. A cash infusion poured into the old sprawl would have fed the same contradictions. The strategic force came from the fit between diagnosis and action: simplify the line, reduce channels, outsource manufacturing, lower inventory, and stop pretending every product family deserved rescue.

Ask the question in your own setting: what is the condition doing the real damage? Not the embarrassing symptom. Not the public goal. The condition. A team misses release dates because every customer promise is treated as sacred. A clinic misses follow-ups because no one owns the weekend handoff. A library fills the calendar while attendance falls because every program has a defender and no governing audience.

Bad strategy often looks busy because busyness is socially useful. It lets people defend effort without defending fit. A leader can announce alliances, feedback systems, new markets, technical programs, and culture work, then leave the hardest question untouched. What obstacle makes these actions belong together? If no answer appears, the plan may be energetic, but the energy has no center.

Camille learns this after a failed library season. Her program calendar is full, the circulation slips are down, and the locked supply cabinet holds craft materials for six events no one attended. In the postmortem, she stops asking which program needs better promotion. She lays the calendar beside the slips and names the governing problem: too many small events are stealing staff time from the after-school tutoring room that still has a waiting list. The next plan is not more creative. It is more coherent.

There is a limit. Cutting things does not automatically make a strategy good. A retailer can shrink out of fear, a hospital can cancel support that patients need, and a school can drop programs because a budget sheet demands it. Narrowing becomes strategic only when the remaining actions become more mutually reinforcing against the obstacle that matters. If the action gets smaller but no clearer, the organization has only made decline easier to schedule.

That distinction protects the Apple lesson from becoming a worship of cuts. The useful lesson is not smallness. It is coherence under pressure. When the obstacle is sprawl, fewer products and simpler channels can create force. When the obstacle is trust, quality, access, speed, or a missing handoff, the fitting response will look different.

Hugo faces that difference on a SaaS support team. Before the change, every customer complaint became a product promise, every promise became a feature flag, and the refund queue kept growing. After one support transcript is read aloud, he stops the meeting and reorders the work. First: stop promising custom fixes. Second: repair the two failure paths already hurting renewals. Third: tell sales what cannot be sold this quarter. The action feels narrower, but the team finally has a center.

That is what separates good strategy from strategy-shaped busyness. One accepts the pain of choosing. The other keeps every hopeful verb alive and calls the pile momentum.

examples.title: Rebecca Crosses Out the Repair-Counter Extras
examples.scenario: The service-ticket printout sits where the laptop was supposed to go at the Tuesday regional review. Rebecca, the repair lead, has a cracked phone shell in one hand and an inventory aging report in the other. The table wants six fixes: new signage, longer hours, a training clip, a warranty script, a parts app, and a weekend promo. She has to decide whether to protect the list or cross out every item that does not reduce the nine-day parts delay.
examples.whatToDo: Put the printout at the center, name the parts delay as the governing obstacle, and cut every proposed action that does not shorten that wait.
examples.whyItMatters: The team cannot create force while six answers compete. Once the obstacle is visible, each action can be judged by fit instead of by how responsible it sounds.

examples.title: Thomas Deletes the Extra Weekend Checklist
examples.scenario: "Show me which part this fixes," Thomas says at the Friday discharge huddle, holding up the new checklist beside the nurse callback log. The Saturday staffing grid is open on the charge nurse desk. Two proposals are fighting for the same hour: a second checklist review or one named weekend handoff owner. Thomas must decide before the huddle ends whether to keep both safe-looking actions or delete the weaker one in front of the team.
examples.whatToDo: Force the choice. Keep the named handoff owner if the callback log shows ownership is the failure, and remove the second checklist review from the plan.
examples.whyItMatters: Two plausible fixes can weaken each other when they answer different diagnoses. Choosing one lets weekend staff know what problem they are solving.

examples.title: Camille Finds the Calendar’s Real Drag
examples.scenario: The room smells faintly of toner and rain-soaked coats after the trustees leave. Camille spreads the program calendar beside circulation slips from the past quarter and a photo of the locked supply cabinet. The failed slate looked busy on paper: author nights, craft sessions, coding club, film talks. In the postmortem she marks the hidden constraint in red: every small event stole staff from the tutoring desk families actually used.
examples.whatToDo: Use the calendar and slips to name staff fragmentation as the obstacle, then cut programs that do not support the tutoring demand already visible.
examples.whyItMatters: The old slate failed because activity was mistaken for coherence. The evidence shows which demand should govern the next set of choices.

examples.title: Lukas Marks the One Robotics Path
examples.scenario: You can see the weak spot before anyone names it: three half-built robots, one robotics kit crate, and a competition rule sheet taped to the lab door. "We can enter both divisions," a parent says. Lukas taps the battery tester on the crate. "Then which machine gets the good batteries for the final month?" The club must choose before registration closes whether to chase two trophies or build one reliable machine.
examples.whatToDo: Mark one competition path on the rule sheet and assign the best parts, practice slots, and batteries to that path only.
examples.whyItMatters: A vague goal lets every hope stay alive. A named path makes the scarce parts reinforce one result instead of being spread across two weak entries.

examples.title: Aanya Tests the Import Plan Against Spoilage
examples.scenario: It took Aanya three weeks to stop trusting the clean version of the plan. The customs invoice looked harmless on her office counter, until a spoiled cheese sample arrived warm and the cash-flow calendar showed two more shipments due before payment cleared. Her sales manager wants a larger order to impress retailers. Aanya has to decide whether to predict demand from interest or test the plan against spoilage and cash first.
examples.whatToDo: Place the invoice, sample, and cash calendar together, then reject any order size that does not solve the delay between customs, shelf life, and payment.
examples.whyItMatters: The real obstacle is not retailer interest. It is the mismatch between cash timing and spoiled inventory, so growth talk only makes the weakness larger.

examples.title: Hugo Reorders the Product-Promise Meeting
examples.scenario: What changes when the constraint is placed in the open? On Monday, Hugo’s SaaS support team starts with a feature flag list and ends with twelve promises nobody owns. On Thursday, he reads one support transcript beside the refund queue and stops the meeting. Before the roadmap review continues, he rearranges the sequence: first stop custom promises, then fix the two failure paths, then tell sales what cannot be sold this quarter.
examples.whatToDo: Lead with the support transcript and refund queue, then reorder the meeting around the failure path instead of the feature list.
examples.whyItMatters: The old meeting protected promises. The new order makes the obstacle govern the work, so product and sales stop adding contradictions.

questions.prompt: A regional gym chain has a plan that lists new classes, a referral drive, lobby paint, instructor training, and a pricing test. Cancellations are rising because evening classes start late. Which response best fits good strategy?
choices: Name late starts as the governing obstacle, then align staffing, room turnover, and class scheduling around fixing that delay.
Keep all five initiatives because each one could improve the member experience in a different way.
Set a more ambitious retention goal so every department feels the urgency of the problem.
questions.explanation: The correct choice names the obstacle and coordinates action around it. Keeping every initiative preserves clutter, while a bigger goal adds pressure without diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A college dining service blames low satisfaction on weak marketing, but comment cards show students leave when the allergen station runs out by noon. What should the director do first?
choices: Launch a campus campaign explaining the quality of the dining program.
Treat the noon allergen shortage as the real obstacle and redirect purchasing, prep, and staff checks toward that station.
Add more menu experiments so students see that the dining team is innovating.
questions.explanation: The station shortage is the obstacle that should govern action. Marketing and menu experiments may sound active, but neither answers the failure students actually feel.

questions.prompt: A repair shop owner wants to respond to slipping margins by buying ads, adding Saturday hours, and launching a loyalty card. The parts shelf shows the same three components are always missing. What is the soundest move?
choices: Buy ads first because more volume will cover the margin problem.
Add the loyalty card first because repeat customers are cheaper to retain.
Use the parts shortage as the diagnosis and coordinate ordering, supplier terms, and technician scheduling around it.
questions.explanation: The missing components explain the margin leak and should shape the response. Ads or loyalty work could increase demand while leaving the core delay untouched.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit board approves a plan with ten priorities after a quiet retreat. The only hard data says donor renewals drop after delayed thank-you calls. What should a new director challenge?
choices: Whether ten priorities are hiding from the renewal obstacle rather than answering it.
Whether the retreat needed more diverse voices before the priorities were approved.
Whether the thank-you call team should use warmer language in its scripts.
questions.explanation: The issue is fit: the priorities do not show how they answer the renewal delay. Broader voices or warmer scripts may help later, but they do not test coherence.

questions.prompt: A city parks team says its strategy is to increase usage, modernize facilities, improve inclusion, build partnerships, and upgrade signage. Weekend field permits are the only service with a waitlist. What is the best critique?
choices: The plan has too few numeric targets to guide accountability.
The plan sounds broad but has not named the obstacle that should organize its choices.
The plan should prioritize partnerships because partners can share the cost burden.
questions.explanation: The critique is that the plan has no governing problem. Numeric targets and partners can be useful, but they do not substitute for a diagnosis.

questions.prompt: A medical device startup says it will win through bold culture, fast hiring, international expansion, and constant customer listening. Lab notes show sterilization failures are delaying every pilot. Which option shows coherent action?
choices: Pause expansion hiring, assign engineering to sterilization reliability, and make pilots depend on passing that test.
Keep hiring fast because more engineers will eventually solve the sterilization issue.
Begin international expansion early so one market delay does not stop the company.
questions.explanation: This action lets the sterilization obstacle govern hiring and pilots. The other choices add motion while the one failure controlling progress remains unresolved.

questions.prompt: A school principal inherits a plan full of slogans about excellence and belonging. Attendance records show ninth graders miss the first period after late bus arrivals. What would make the plan strategic?
choices: Replacing the slogans with a shorter inspirational statement that staff can remember.
Building a coordinated response around buses, first-period scheduling, family contact, and ninth-grade monitoring.
Creating a committee to collect more values from teachers and families.
questions.explanation: The coordinated response fits the actual attendance obstacle. A better slogan or broader values process may feel inclusive, but neither organizes action around the cause.

questions.prompt: A bakery cuts its wholesale line after seeing that retail customers spend more per order. Two months later, staff have fewer shifts and retail still misses daily targets because morning production is late. How should you evaluate the cut?
choices: It was strategic because cutting any line creates focus.
It was strategic because retail has a higher average order value.
It was not yet strategic because the cut did not address the production delay that controlled retail performance.
questions.explanation: Narrowing counts only when it improves coherence around the real obstacle. Higher order value and fewer lines do not matter if late production still controls results.

questions.prompt: A software team has three proposals after churn rises: add onboarding videos, discount annual plans, and hire customer success reps. Exit interviews show customers leave after one broken data import. What should guide the choice?
choices: Which proposal is fastest to announce to customers.
Which proposal best coordinates product, support, and sales around fixing the import failure.
Which proposal is cheapest this quarter.
questions.explanation: The import failure is the obstacle that should organize the response across functions. Speed and cost matter, but they are secondary if the action misses the reason customers leave.

reviewCards.front: A plan has many energetic initiatives but no named obstacle. What should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Ask what problem governs the plan. If no single obstacle explains why the actions belong together, the plan is still activity, not coherent strategy.

reviewCards.front: A leader proposes cutting three projects. What condition makes the cut strategic instead of mere retreat?
reviewCards.back: The cut must make the remaining actions reinforce one another against the real obstacle. Smaller is not enough; clearer and more coherent is the test.

reviewCards.front: Your team wants to protect every popular action in a turnaround plan. What is the retrieval move?
reviewCards.back: Name the diagnosis, then test each action against it. Actions that do not answer the diagnosis lose protection, even if they sound responsible.

reviewCards.front: Why can a polished list of alliances, systems, and market pushes still be bad strategy?
reviewCards.back: Because the list may never name the obstacle that makes the actions fit. Strategy needs a governing problem and coordinated response, not just serious nouns.

reviewCards.front: What does Apple in 1997 help you remember about strategy under pressure?
reviewCards.back: The useful lesson is coherence. Jobs narrowed products, channels, software work, manufacturing, and inventory around the problem of sprawl, so the actions added force.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice turning plans into governed choices. Name the obstacle first, choose the response second, and let actions survive only if they reinforce that response.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a planning meeting starts collecting initiatives, then write the suspected obstacle at the top of the page and ask which actions would still matter if that obstacle ruled the decision.
If an action sounds popular but does not fit the diagnosis, then mark it as deferred instead of letting it stay on the plan as a protected extra.
If a group project has too many deliverables, then choose the one failure that would sink the grade and align roles around preventing it.
If your own plan keeps expanding, then name the bottleneck and remove one task that creates motion without reducing it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, take one plan you can influence and rewrite it as three bullets: obstacle, chosen response, coherent action. Remove one action that does not fit.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit a live plan for clutter. Circle the governing obstacle, underline the actions that directly answer it, and move the rest to a separate parking list.

memorableLines.text: Good strategy starts where the real obstacle is named.
A real diagnosis changes the room.
Good strategy is governed choice.

chapters.title: Discovering Power
chapters.hook: The strongest player in the room may be weak the moment the game changes shape.
chapters.counterintuition: Visible strength can look like power, but actually hide the condition that changes the contest. Strategic power appears where the rules of the fight can shift.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one fight you are entering today. Write the opponent’s preferred terms, then write one way to change the contest so your own strength matters more.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Strategic power appears when you stop matching the visible fight and find the asymmetry, system, or cost shift that changes what strength means.

breakdown.fastRead:
Megan lays the scoring strip on the gym floor before practice starts. Her tallest fencer keeps losing to a faster boy because every bout is becoming a straight-line rush. Megan moves the strip closer to the wall, changes the drill, and asks where the faster boy can no longer use distance. The lesson is immediate: power was not in trying harder inside the old bout. It was in changing the bout.

David and Goliath carries the same logic. David wins strategic power by changing the contest the stronger side expects. A weaker player becomes dangerous when the contest no longer rewards the giant's preferred strength.
breakdown.deepRead:
Julien studies a pole map for a rural broadband cooperative while the room argues about marketing and sign-up discounts. The trenching invoice tells a different story. The cost driver is not demand; it is the last mile of digging through rock before winter. Julien deletes the discount campaign from the board and circles the weather window. The cooperative has to win by sequencing crews where each new pole lowers the next install cost.

Hidden power is often structural.

Wal-Mart network power was not a store trick to copy. The force sat in the reinforcing system behind the store: locations, logistics, information, and repetition working together. A rival copying shelf labels or greeters would miss the engine. It would imitate the visible surface while leaving the system advantage untouched.

David and Goliath is the older version of the same lesson: David wins strategic power by rejecting the giant's preferred contest. That is why discovering power comes before using force. You can spend the same money, hire the same people, and copy the same visible moves while gaining none of the advantage. Power lives in the relationship between pieces. Sometimes it sits in a bottleneck. Sometimes it sits in cost asymmetry. Sometimes it sits in a rule the other side depends on but you can refuse.

The weak player is not automatically clever. The weak player only gains power after finding the condition that changes the contest.
breakdown.fullRead:
Astrid finds the hidden power of a university newspaper only after the rumor channel beats her twice. The newsroom wants more posts, a sharper social feed, and a faster headline process. Then she opens the anonymous tip inbox and matches three tips to locations on the campus map. The rumor accounts are fast, but they cannot verify. The newspaper has student reporters inside dorm councils, lab groups, and budget meetings. Speed is not the winning contest. Verified access is.

This is the shift that turns power from a noun into a search. Do not ask only who has more money, more staff, or more reach. Ask what condition would make those strengths less decisive. Ask what your side can do repeatedly, cheaply, or credibly that the other side finds expensive to match. Ask where the visible contest is misleading you.

Marshall and Roche strategy against the Soviet Union used that kind of asymmetric-cost logic. The aim was not to match weapon system for weapon system as if the scoreboard were simple symmetry. The sharper question was which American technological strengths could force the Soviet side into more costly responses. Power came from making the other side pay heavily to keep up.

You can use the same lens in smaller settings. Diego sits with a defense contractor bid team that wants to promise better performance on every feature. The test range slot is the scarce asset. A prototype casing sits cracked beside a cost-response chart, and Diego asks which demonstration would force rivals into extra retesting. The bid becomes less about claiming superiority everywhere and more about making speed through testing the pressure point.

A common objection says this sounds like cleverness dressed as strategy. That is a fair worry. Tricks fade once the other side sees them. Hidden power is different because it rests on a condition that can be reinforced: a network, a cost structure, a privileged access point, a timing window, a rule change, or a repeated capability. If the move works only once because it surprises, treat it as a tactic. If it changes what the contest rewards and can be strengthened, it may be power.

Kiran sees the difference in an independent pharmacy network. A single pharmacy cannot beat the national chain on price or advertising. The delivery bins, route magnets, and prescription bags reveal another possibility. Coordinated deliveries to care homes let six small stores create density the chain's broad route does not match. The power is not the van. It is the network pattern the van can serve.

Claire finds it in a public defender office. Before the change, every attorney complains about overload. After she lays the court docket beside case folders and intake timestamps, she sees that late intake review, not hearing preparation, is the choke point. The office stops matching pressure with more heroic hours and changes the docket flow. The same lawyers gain power because the contest changes from endurance to sequence.

Power is discovered when the obvious scoreboard stops being treated as the truth.

examples.title: Megan Moves the Strip Near the Wall
examples.scenario: The scoring strip sits on the gym floor at 6:10 p.m., pulled two meters closer to the wall than usual. Megan, the youth fencing coach, holds a foil mask under one arm while the bout bracket shows her shortest fencer facing the club’s fastest attacker. She is about to decide whether to drill faster retreats or change the strip position so the attacker’s preferred distance disappears.
examples.whatToDo: Change the bout condition first. Make the attacker fence in a space where the smaller fencer’s timing and angle matter more than straight-line speed.
examples.whyItMatters: The old contest rewards the rival’s strength. Moving the constraint changes what wins, which is where hidden power begins.

examples.title: Julien Circles the Rock Trench
examples.scenario: "Show me which mile this fixes," Julien says in the cooperative office, sliding the pole map over the trenching invoice. The weather window closes in three weeks. One proposal discounts sign-ups across the valley; the other clusters crews along the rocky ridge first. Julien has to decide whether to protect the popular campaign or delete it and aim every crew at the cost driver.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the ridge, cancel the broad discount, and sequence crews where each completed pole lowers the next install cost.
examples.whyItMatters: The cooperative gains power by changing the cost curve, not by attracting demand it cannot serve cheaply once winter hits.

examples.title: Astrid Maps the Rumor Advantage Backward
examples.scenario: The basement newsroom smells of toner and wet wool after the student senate meeting. Astrid opens the anonymous tip inbox beside the print deadline board and campus map. The paper lost two stories to rumor accounts last week, and the staff blamed speed. In the postmortem, she pins each missed tip to a dorm, lab, or council room and sees the hidden constraint: they have access the rumor feeds cannot verify.
examples.whatToDo: Build the plan around verified access. Assign reporters to the tip locations and stop trying to beat rumor accounts on raw posting speed.
examples.whyItMatters: The paper’s power is credibility tied to place. Chasing speed copies the rival’s game and wastes the advantage already inside the newsroom.

examples.title: Diego Chooses the Test That Raises Rival Costs
examples.scenario: You can see the weak spot before anyone names it: one test range slot, a dented prototype casing, and a cost-response chart on Diego’s desk. "Promise more features," the sales lead says. Diego taps the slot confirmation. "Or prove the casing survives the drop they cannot retest before bid day." The team must choose before noon whether to look broad or make rivals pay to respond.
examples.whatToDo: Use the test slot on the demonstration rivals cannot cheaply repeat, and make that proof the center of the bid.
examples.whyItMatters: The leverage is not a bigger promise. It is a test that changes the response cost for everyone else in the contest.

examples.title: Kiran Tests the Route Density Guess
examples.scenario: Only after the third missed care-home delivery on a wet Thursday at the Ottawa pharmacy hub does Kiran, the delivery manager, trust the route magnets more than the tidy delivery report. The bins look evenly loaded, but the back-office map shows three care homes could share one dense loop before noon. He has to choose between adding a van or rebuilding the care-home route around that density. In the pharmacy dispatch room, the 10 a.m. care-home medication window makes the route choice concrete rather than a general delivery improvement.
examples.whatToDo: Group the care-home deliveries, measure the route time, and build the network around dense stops before promising broader coverage.
examples.whyItMatters: A small pharmacy network cannot outspend a chain. It can create power when coordination makes each stop cheaper than a scattered route.

examples.title: Claire Moves Intake Before the Docket Fight
examples.scenario: What changes when the docket stops looking like one long emergency? On Tuesday morning, Claire’s office starts with case folders stacked by hearing date and ends with everyone asking for more prep hours. On Friday, she lays the court docket beside intake timestamps and stops the meeting. Before the next calendar call, she moves intake review ahead of hearing prep so late facts stop poisoning every file downstream.
examples.whatToDo: Reorder the workflow around intake review, then protect hearing preparation only after the late-fact choke point is fixed.
examples.whyItMatters: The office gains power by changing sequence. More hours in the old flow would keep feeding the same docket failure.

questions.prompt: A small soccer club keeps losing to richer clubs that recruit faster players. Its coach notices the home field is narrow and rewards set pieces. What response shows hidden power?
choices: Run more conditioning so players can match the richer clubs’ speed.
Build training around throws, corners, and compact defending that make the narrow field matter.
Raise money for one star forward so the club can compete on talent.
questions.explanation: The narrow field changes what strength means. Conditioning or buying a forward keeps the club inside the richer rival’s preferred contest.

questions.prompt: A local grocer cannot match a national chain’s prices, but it knows apartment managers who need predictable weekly deliveries. Which action best discovers power?
choices: Map delivery density around those buildings and offer reliable scheduled drops the chain does not coordinate.
Run a broad price-matching campaign for the whole neighborhood.
Copy the chain’s shelf layout to look more professional.
questions.explanation: The manager relationships and delivery density create a different contest. Price matching and shelf copying imitate the chain where it is already stronger.

questions.prompt: A university lab competes for grants against famous institutions. It owns a rare microscope with open weekend capacity. What should guide its proposal?
choices: Emphasize that the lab will work harder despite having less prestige.
List all prior publications to look as broad as the famous institutions.
Design the proposal around fast weekend access to the microscope that larger labs cannot easily offer.
questions.explanation: The microscope access is an asymmetry that changes the basis of competition. Effort and breadth keep the lab trapped in the prestige contest.

questions.prompt: A regional courier is losing urban accounts to a larger rival. Its route data show it reaches remote clinics twice as reliably during storms. What is the strategic implication?
choices: The courier should discount city accounts until volume returns.
The courier should focus on storm-reliable clinic routes where the rival’s size does not translate into dependability.
The courier should buy more trucks so it looks closer to the larger rival.
questions.explanation: Storm reliability in remote routes is a condition where the smaller firm’s pattern matters. Discounts and trucks chase the rival’s scale game.

questions.prompt: A cybersecurity firm cannot outstaff a major competitor, but its tool updates rules within minutes because engineers sit beside analysts. Which choice uses that power?
choices: Promise a wider service catalog so buyers see the firm as full scale.
Hire a large sales team before improving the tool.
Sell rapid rule updates for active incidents, where speed of analyst-to-engineer learning matters most.
questions.explanation: The fast analyst-engineer loop is the hidden power. Wider catalog claims and sales hiring add surface scale without using the firm’s real advantage.

questions.prompt: A café near a train station cannot beat chains on brand recognition. It can serve commuters in three minutes because the kitchen is beside the pickup window. What would be a weak imitation?
choices: Advertising commuter pickup with a strict three-minute menu.
Redesigning prep around the pickup window and removing slow items.
Copying the chain’s loyalty app and seasonal drink calendar.
questions.explanation: The loyalty app and drink calendar copy visible chain practices. The café’s power sits in its layout and speed window, which the other options reinforce.

questions.prompt: A public school debate team always loses to private schools with more coaches. It notices judges reward evidence packets that arrive before rounds. What should it do?
choices: Train students to speak faster so they seem more prepared.
Use volunteer parents to prepare and deliver cleaner evidence packets before each round.
Enter more tournaments to gain general experience.
questions.explanation: The evidence-packet routine changes the contest away from coaching depth. Speaking faster and more tournaments leave the team in the private schools’ strength zone.

questions.prompt: A startup says it has discovered power because a launch stunt went viral once. Three months later competitors copy the stunt. How should you evaluate the claim?
choices: It is power because the first stunt produced attention.
It is power only if the stunt can be repeated under different conditions.
It was more likely a tactic because it did not rest on a reinforcing condition rivals found costly to match.
questions.explanation: A one-time surprise is not the same as a durable asymmetry. The test is whether the move changes response costs or can be reinforced.

questions.prompt: A regional bank wants to beat national banks on mobile features. Its strongest asset is a loan officer network trusted by local contractors. What question should come first?
choices: How can the bank build every mobile feature the national banks advertise?
How can the contractor network create a loan experience national banks cannot cheaply copy?
How can the bank make its app look more modern before the next campaign?
questions.explanation: The contractor network may change the contest from app breadth to trusted local lending. Copying features or app styling follows the national banks’ visible game.

reviewCards.front: A smaller player faces a bigger rival. What is the first strategic question?
reviewCards.back: Ask what condition could make the rival’s size matter less. Hidden power appears when the contest changes and a different strength becomes decisive.

reviewCards.front: Why does copying a visible store practice often miss the source of power?
reviewCards.back: The visible practice may only be the surface of a reinforcing system. If the power sits in a network, copying one store habit gives you the sign without the engine.

reviewCards.front: A team has one clever surprise move. What test separates tactic from power?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the move rests on a condition that can be reinforced and is costly for rivals to match. If it works only because it was unexpected once, treat it as a tactic.

reviewCards.front: What does the David and Goliath anchor help you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Refuse the opponent’s preferred terms. David’s power comes from changing the contest so the giant’s strength is less decisive.

reviewCards.front: How can asymmetric cost become strategic power?
reviewCards.back: Choose a response that makes the other side pay more to keep up than you pay to act. The contest shifts because the cost of matching becomes uneven.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice looking under the visible contest. Name the opponent’s preferred terms, then search for an asymmetry, network, cost shift, timing window, or access point that changes what strength means.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a larger rival defines the comparison, then write down the comparison and ask which condition would make that comparison less important.
If the room wants to copy a visible practice, then ask what system behind that practice creates the advantage and whether you can build any part of that system.
If the other side wants a direct contest of resources, then look for a rule, deadline, or cost response that makes matching you expensive.
If you feel outmatched, then list the one thing you can do repeatedly or cheaply that the stronger side cannot easily copy.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, take one rivalry or constraint you face and write two columns: their preferred contest and your possible asymmetry. Choose one action from the second column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one decision by asking where power actually sits: scale, network, timing, access, cost asymmetry, sequence, or credibility. Record the answer before choosing action.

memorableLines.text: Hidden power is often structural.
Power is discovered when the obvious scoreboard stops being treated as the truth.
The weak player is not automatically clever.

chapters.title: Bad Strategy
chapters.hook: The most dangerous plan in the room may be the one with the cleanest verbs.
chapters.counterintuition: Activity gets the credit when a plan looks serious. Diagnosis is doing the work that separates strategy from a protected pile of initiatives.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open one current plan and underline every action verb. If the verbs do not point to one named obstacle, write “missing diagnosis” in the margin.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Bad strategy hides in attractive language when goals, initiatives, and confidence replace diagnosis, tradeoff, and a choice that can actually guide action.

breakdown.fastRead:
Anna props the poster mockup against a stack of budget sheets. The student government slogan says “One Campus, One Voice,” but the petition sheet beside it is empty. Every proposed project sounds friendly. None explains why students stopped attending open meetings. Anna crosses out the spirit week, the video wall, and the branded hoodies until only one question remains: what obstacle are they answering?

Bad strategy often wears good manners. It says growth, excellence, transformation, or community while refusing to choose.

The warning sign is not weakness. It is missing logic. A plan can be loud, polished, and optimistic while still having no diagnosis, no tradeoff, and no leverage.
breakdown.deepRead:
Martin stands in the museum’s member office with a wall chart that shows twelve initiatives and one flat renewal line. The donor call list says lapsed members want evening access. The gallery floor plan says the only evening guard slot is already committed to private rentals. Martin asks the team to choose: protect the rental revenue or rebuild membership around one evening each week.

A bad strategy often fails before execution begins.

It fails because nobody has allowed a real choice to govern the work. The initiative pile offers safety. Each item has a sponsor, a moral appeal, or a plausible metric. Together they make the room feel active without giving anyone a reason to stop doing what does not fit.

Fluff is one signal. Goals without policy are another. A third is leverage blindness: the plan talks about effort while missing the specific point where effort could matter most. These failures can appear in one document or in one meeting. They share the same shape. Language is doing work that diagnosis should have done.

Sophie sees it after a regional bank’s transformation deck fails. The slides promised simplicity, digital trust, local relationships, and new risk tools. The branch heat map and risk register showed the real problem: small-business loan approvals stalled in two rural branches because compliance review arrived late. The deck had many virtues. It still had no center.
breakdown.fullRead:
Jonas sits with a housing coalition that wants to fight evictions, lobby the city, recruit volunteers, publish tenant guides, and prepare a grant proposal. The tenant map shows one neighborhood where notices are clustering. The grant deadline is six days away. A stack of eviction notices sits on the table with names blacked out. Jonas asks which door the coalition will knock on first, and the room goes quiet.

That quiet is useful. Bad strategy survives in rooms that never go quiet because nobody asks the question that would force exclusion. The softer questions are easier: What should we value? What would look bold? Which initiative deserves mention? The harder question is sharper: what must lose protection because it does not answer the obstacle?

You can test for bad strategy without being cynical. Look for a missing diagnosis. Look for goals that float above any chosen policy. Look for activity lists that let every department, committee, or faction keep its favorite work. Look for confidence that rises exactly where evidence thins out. Those are not personality flaws. They are structural symptoms of a plan that wants the benefits of strategy without the cost of choice.

Layla’s product team hits the same wall. The roadmap board has twenty-seven feature cards. The bug queue has three failures that account for most refund requests. The launch calendar is full because each account manager added one client promise. Layla runs a quick prediction: if every feature ships, what failure disappears? The answer is none. She removes the client-request pile and marks the three refund bugs as the governing work.

The temptation is to call this an execution problem. That label is often too generous. Execution can fail a good strategy, but bad strategy can also create execution theater. People work hard on pieces that were never joined by a real diagnosis. They miss deadlines because every deadline survived. They argue about resources because no choice has told the organization what deserves resources first.

There is also a tone problem. Bad strategy borrows the sound of intelligence. It uses broad nouns, brave adjectives, and enough action verbs to seem managerial. That is why it can pass a first reading. You have to ask what the language is protecting. If it protects everyone’s preferred work, suspect evasion. If it exposes the tradeoff, suspect strategy.

Ben learns this in an airport food vendor plan. Before the change, the menu mockups chase business travelers, families, flight crews, and tourists at once. Passenger counts show the real constraint: the terminal lease gives him a narrow breakfast window near two commuter gates. After placing the lease beside the counts, he stops designing for everyone and builds a fast breakfast counter for the passengers already passing in volume.

Bad strategy is not a plan that fails. It is a plan that avoids the work a real plan must do. It will not name what hurts. It will not choose what matters. It will not use the leverage already sitting in the situation. It can still sound excellent in a meeting. That is why you need the artifact on the table, the obstacle in plain words, and the courage to remove the verbs that do not belong.

examples.title: Anna Cuts the Slogan Projects
examples.scenario: The poster mockup leans against the student-union window before Monday lunch, bright with the slogan One Campus, One Voice. Anna, the student president, lays the budget spreadsheet beside an empty petition sheet. The council is about to approve hoodies, a video wall, and spirit week. She has to decide whether to protect the upbeat slate or cross out every item that does not explain why meeting turnout collapsed.
examples.whatToDo: Put the empty petition sheet beside the poster, name turnout as the missing diagnosis, and cut the projects that only decorate the slogan.
examples.whyItMatters: The council does not need more friendly verbs. It needs one problem that can govern spending and make the remaining actions fit.

examples.title: Martin Deletes the Gallery Giveaway
examples.scenario: "Which member are we trying to bring back?" Martin asks in the museum office, pointing to the membership wall chart. The donor call list says lapsed members want evening access; the gallery floor plan shows staff already assigned to a private rental. The team must choose before the budget file closes: fund another giveaway or protect one weekly evening opening for members.
examples.whatToDo: Delete the giveaway, choose the lapsed-member obstacle, and move staff time toward a weekly evening that the renewal calls actually support.
examples.whyItMatters: Twelve initiatives can hide from one tradeoff. Renewal work needs a choice about access, not more disconnected gestures.

examples.title: Sophie Finds the Missing Bank Obstacle
examples.scenario: The stale smell of reheated coffee hangs in the branch training room after the transformation launch misses its first target. Sophie spreads the slide deck beside a branch heat map and risk register. The deck promised digital trust and local service. The postmortem shows rural small-business loans stalled in two branches because compliance review arrived late. The hidden constraint was never named.
examples.whatToDo: Use the heat map and risk register to replace the transformation language with the compliance-review obstacle that actually slowed loan approvals.
examples.whyItMatters: The deck sounded strategic because it used confident nouns. The artifacts show the work had no governing problem.

examples.title: Jonas Forces the Housing Tradeoff
examples.scenario: You can see the weak spot on the tenant map before anyone admits it. Notices cluster around two blocks, while the grant deadline and eviction letters sit on Jonas’s desk. "We can lobby, canvass, and publish the guide," one organizer says. Jonas circles the two blocks. "Before Friday, which door do we knock on first?" The coalition must choose between broad concern and one tractable intervention.
examples.whatToDo: Circle the notice cluster, choose the first two blocks, and let the grant language follow that intervention instead of every wish the coalition holds.
examples.whyItMatters: Avoiding tradeoffs feels generous, but it leaves tenants with scattered help. A marked place turns concern into a choice.

examples.title: Layla Tests the Feature Pile
examples.scenario: By the second refund meeting in the SaaS support room, Layla the product lead has stopped believing the roadmap board. Twenty-seven feature cards fill it, while the bug queue shows three import failures driving the refund spike. She must decide whether to keep the launch calendar or halt feature work until the import path is fixed. The refund queue is still open on the support monitor, so the choice has to change today's import failures before another feature card is added.
examples.whatToDo: Run the prediction against the refund queue, then remove feature cards that do not reduce the three import failures.
examples.whyItMatters: The roadmap is hiding leverage blindness. If the work does not touch the refund driver, it is activity with product labels.

examples.title: Ben Narrows the Airport Menu
examples.scenario: Which passenger is the menu really built for in the airport terminal office at 6:40 a.m.? Ben, the restaurant designer, has mockups chasing families, tourists, crews, and executives. Then he places the terminal lease beside passenger counts and must decide whether to narrow the menu around the travelers who actually pass the counter before boarding. The terminal lease renewal is due that afternoon, which forces Ben to pick the passenger group before the menu becomes another compromise.
examples.whatToDo: Let the terminal lease and passenger counts pick the segment, then design the menu sequence around that traffic instead of every imagined traveler.
examples.whyItMatters: Serving everyone keeps the vendor from using its actual location. The constraint gives the menu a center.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit plan promises awareness, partnerships, youth engagement, digital reach, and policy change. It never says why donations have fallen. What is the clearest sign of bad strategy?
choices: The plan contains too many nonprofit activities to finish in one year.
The plan uses goals and initiatives while avoiding the diagnosis that should guide them.
The plan should have included more aggressive fundraising targets.
questions.explanation: The failure is not merely length. The plan avoids the reason donations fell, so the actions cannot be judged by fit.

questions.prompt: A school improvement plan says every student will thrive, every teacher will innovate, and every family will feel heard. Attendance data show ninth-grade absences drive most failures. What should happen first?
choices: Replace the slogans with a diagnosis of ninth-grade absence and choose actions that directly reduce it.
Keep the slogans because broad language helps every group feel included.
Add a morale campaign so teachers feel inspired to act.
questions.explanation: The attendance problem should govern action. Inclusive slogans and morale work may sound positive, but they leave the controlling obstacle vague.

questions.prompt: A product leader presents ten feature launches as the strategy for reducing churn. Support tickets show customers leave after failed data imports. Which critique is strongest?
choices: Ten launches are too many for customers to understand.
The leader should put the features in a simpler visual format.
The feature list has no policy for the churn obstacle shown in the support tickets.
questions.explanation: The feature pile may look active, but it misses the import failure that controls churn. Design clarity would not fix the missing logic.

questions.prompt: A city agency calls its plan “A Cleaner, Safer, Smarter Downtown” and funds murals, patrols, bins, cameras, and events. Complaint logs show trash pickup fails after weekend festivals. What action best exposes bad strategy?
choices: Ask which funded actions directly fix post-festival pickup and pause the rest until the obstacle is named.
Ask communications to make the slogan more concrete for residents.
Add a sixth initiative focused on volunteer pride.
questions.explanation: The complaint logs reveal a governing obstacle. The other choices improve language or add activity while leaving the pickup failure in place.

questions.prompt: A hospital service line misses targets, and leaders respond with a culture campaign, a patient app, a referral lunch, and new posters. Nurse notes show delays start at one intake desk. What pattern is visible?
choices: Leaders are using strategy-free activity to avoid a specific operational diagnosis.
The hospital needs a more optimistic vision before staff can act.
The intake desk should be ignored until the culture campaign has time to work.
questions.explanation: The activity pile hides from the intake diagnosis. Optimism and patience do not make the scattered actions coherent.

questions.prompt: A museum team votes to keep all twelve membership initiatives because each one has a passionate sponsor. Renewal calls point to one missing evening-access option. What should a strategist do?
choices: Rank initiatives by sponsor enthusiasm.
Keep all twelve to preserve morale during implementation.
Make evening access the diagnosis and remove initiatives that do not support renewal.
questions.explanation: Sponsor passion is not a strategic test. The renewal evidence supplies the obstacle, and unfitting work must lose protection.

questions.prompt: A startup says its strategy is “win enterprise,” then lists security, onboarding, integrations, brand, conferences, and hiring. Sales losses trace to one procurement security question. What does the phrase “win enterprise” lack?
choices: A longer explanation of the market opportunity.
A diagnosis and guiding policy that would decide which actions matter first.
A more memorable internal slogan for the sales team.
questions.explanation: The phrase names an ambition but not the obstacle or response. More explanation or a better slogan would still leave priority unresolved.

questions.prompt: A regional airline cuts snacks, lounge access, and customer service hours after losses. It calls the cuts a strategy. Customer data show losses come from unreliable early flights. How should you evaluate the claim?
choices: The cuts are strategic because they show management is serious.
The cuts are strategic because they reduce cost quickly.
The cuts are weak strategy if they do not address early-flight reliability, the obstacle controlling demand.
questions.explanation: Cost cuts can be useful, but they are not strategy unless they fit the diagnosis. Here the demand problem points to reliability.

questions.prompt: A department head avoids choosing between two projects by approving both and calling the result a portfolio strategy. Both require the same specialist. What question should a colleague ask?
choices: Which project best answers the named obstacle, and which one should lose the specialist for now?
Can the specialist work longer hours during the first month?
Can both projects be described under a broader theme?
questions.explanation: The specialist constraint forces a tradeoff. Longer hours and broader themes preserve the evasion instead of making the strategy choose.

reviewCards.front: A plan has many initiatives and no diagnosis. What should you ask first?
reviewCards.back: Call out the missing diagnosis. Bad strategy often hides behind goals and initiatives when no problem has been allowed to govern action.

reviewCards.front: What does an initiative pile usually protect?
reviewCards.back: It protects people from choosing. Each item may sound reasonable, but the pile lets the room avoid deciding which obstacle matters and which work should stop.

reviewCards.front: How can fluff differ from a real guiding policy?
reviewCards.back: Fluff sounds serious but does not tell anyone what to do or stop doing. A guiding policy narrows action by answering a diagnosis.

reviewCards.front: A team says execution failed, but every priority survived. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Execution may not be the main issue. If every priority survived, the work may have been bad strategy from the start because no tradeoff governed resources.

reviewCards.front: A team copies a famous leverage story without finding its own power source. What blindness is showing?
reviewCards.back: It is talking about effort while missing the specific point where effort would matter most. The plan stays busy and never uses the advantage or bottleneck already visible.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Learn to hear when strategic language is substituting for strategic logic. The practical skill is to find the missing diagnosis, the avoided tradeoff, and the point of leverage the plan refuses to use.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a plan lists many initiatives without one named obstacle, then ask which problem each initiative answers and remove the ones with no answer.
If a team blames execution after every priority was protected, then revisit whether a real tradeoff was ever made.
If consensus arrives too easily, then ask what attractive option the plan has chosen not to do.
If the roadmap grows after every customer complaint, then compare the feature cards with the top failure in the bug queue before approving more work.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, mark one plan for three symptoms: missing diagnosis, initiative pile, and refusal to choose. Rewrite one section so a real tradeoff appears.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, choose one strategy conversation and record the sentence that actually names the obstacle. If no such sentence appears, write the diagnosis the room avoided.

memorableLines.text: Bad strategy often wears good manners.
A bad strategy often fails before execution begins.
Bad strategy borrows the sound of intelligence.

chapters.title: Why So Much Bad Strategy?
chapters.hook: A room can agree quickly because nothing costly has been named yet.
chapters.counterintuition: Avoidance can sound like consensus and still leave the real problem untouched. Bad strategy lets fluff and easy goals stand where diagnosis should be.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one recent consensus decision and write the choice it avoided. Name the group or project that would have lost if the plan had been precise.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Ambiguity keeps bad strategy alive because it buys agreement cheaply, hides political cost, and delays the painful exclusions that real strategy requires.

breakdown.fastRead:
Emily studies the sticky-note wall after a city agency workshop. The notes say access, safety, equity, speed, trust, and innovation. Public comment cards mention one complaint again and again: permit delays for small contractors. The budget cap leaves room for one fix. Emily removes the notes that do not address the delay and watches the room tense up.

That tension explains why bad strategy keeps returning. Vague language lets everyone stay included. Precise diagnosis makes someone pay a cost.

A room may look aligned because nothing has been excluded. The agreement is real, but it is shallow. It lasts only because the hard choice has not arrived.
breakdown.deepRead:
Nicolas holds a cracked machine part at the annual retreat of a family-owned manufacturer. The owner agenda protects new territories, a trade-show booth, a cousin’s custom line, and a service expansion. The part tells a narrower story: field failures are coming from one aging assembly step. Nicolas asks which pet project gets cut so the assembly fix can be funded before the next sales season.

Consensus becomes expensive the moment it meets a constraint.

This is not a story about foolish people. Smart, serious groups often prefer ambiguity because ambiguity performs a social job. It keeps coalitions intact. It lowers the political cost of the meeting. It lets each person hear a version of the plan that protects their own priority. The trouble begins later, when the vague agreement has to become action.

Ingrid sees the aftereffect at a university committee. The committee binder says transformation. The program inventory says duplication. The tuition model says two low-enrollment tracks cannot both survive. In the postmortem, she realizes why the vague language passed so easily: no department had been asked to give anything up.

Bad strategy is often manufactured by the reward system around the room. If precision creates conflict and vagueness creates applause, the room will learn to applaud vagueness.
breakdown.fullRead:
Marco stands in a hospital planning session with a referral queue, a bed map, and a service charter. The charter promises patient-centered excellence across every service line. The referral queue shows orthopedic patients waiting longest. The bed map shows medical patients displaced every Thursday when the operating schedule peaks. Marco asks whether the plan will favor beds for one service line this quarter, and the mood changes.

The mood changes because strategy has touched status. A vague plan lets each service hear respect. A precise plan says which constraint rules and which group absorbs the inconvenience first. People are not irrational for resisting that moment. They are responding to a real political cost.

That is why blaming bad strategy on stupidity misses the mechanism. Many bad plans are produced by capable people who understand exactly which fight a clear diagnosis would start. The institution may not reward them for starting it. It may reward smooth language, broad inclusion, and a document that every stakeholder can endorse before lunch.

You can see the pattern in any committee that loves adjectives. Comprehensive. Transformative. Inclusive. Innovative. Each word may express a genuine value. None forces a choice by itself. The question is what the words are allowed to decide. If they decide nothing, they have become alignment theater.

Yusuf finds that in an arts board funding cycle. The grant score sheets reward ambition, community reach, artistic excellence, access, and experimentation. The rehearsal calendar and donor pledges show that small theater groups are collapsing between grant award and opening night. Yusuf predicts the highest-scoring proposal will again be the broadest. Then he tests it against last year’s canceled productions. Breadth won the scoring meeting; cash timing lost on stage.

A fair objection says consensus is not worthless. True. Strategy often needs cooperation, and a leader who creates needless enemies is not brave. The problem is counterfeit consensus: agreement purchased by leaving the conflict unnamed. Real consensus can survive a stated tradeoff. Counterfeit consensus needs fog.

Grace meets the same fog at a software offsite. Before lunch, every team priority card stays on the table. After she places the dependency board beside the release date, she stops the ranking exercise and changes the order. First choose the dependency that blocks the release. Then choose which team priority waits. Only after that does the roadmap deserve a name.

Ambiguity is attractive because it feels humane. It lets people leave the room believing they were heard. But a plan that hears everyone and chooses nothing has only moved the conflict to a later date, where it will appear as delay, budget creep, missed handoffs, or quiet sabotage.

The cure is not harshness. It is honest specificity. Name the constraint. Name the tradeoff. Name the priority that will wait. A room can still disagree after that, but at least the disagreement is about the real cost. That is progress.

examples.title: Emily Pulls Down the Safe Notes
examples.scenario: The sticky-note wall fills the council annex by four in the afternoon: access, trust, safety, speed, fairness. Emily, the workshop lead, pins public comment cards below it and places the budget cap on the table. Contractors keep naming permit delays. She is about to decide whether to preserve the feel-good clusters or pull down every note that does not address the delay.
examples.whatToDo: Move the budget cap and comment cards into view, name permit delay as the constraint, and remove notes that do not fit that diagnosis.
examples.whyItMatters: The workshop’s agreement is cheap until a constraint appears. Removing safe notes reveals whether the room has strategy or only shared adjectives.

examples.title: Nicolas Cuts the Owner’s Favorite Expansion
examples.scenario: "Which sale survives this defect?" Nicolas asks in the lakeside retreat room, setting a cracked machine part beside the sales territories and the owner agenda. His uncle wants a custom line; his sister wants western expansion. The same technicians are needed for the assembly fix. Nicolas must decide before the retreat vote whether to protect both family projects or delete one from the year plan.
examples.whatToDo: Use the cracked part to force the choice, fund the assembly repair, and remove the expansion that depends on the same scarce technicians.
examples.whyItMatters: Ambiguity keeps family peace until the constraint takes the floor. The part makes the political cost visible enough to choose.

examples.title: Ingrid Reads the Binder Against Tuition
examples.scenario: The seminar room smells of toner and damp coats after the transformation vote passes unanimously. Ingrid opens the committee binder beside the program inventory and tuition model. In the postmortem, she marks the sentence everyone liked: strengthen distinctive learning pathways. Then she marks the hidden constraint: two low-enrollment tracks consume the same faculty load. The phrase passed because no track had to close. The quarterly target packet sits beside the defect log, making the avoidance visible before the team can turn it into another performance slogan.
examples.whatToDo: Read the binder against the tuition model, then replace the broad phrase with the specific track choice the committee avoided.
examples.whyItMatters: Vague transformation language can earn unanimous approval precisely because it leaves the painful exclusion for someone else.

examples.title: Marco Points to the Bed Conflict
examples.scenario: You can see the weak spot in the referral queue before the service chiefs speak. Marco has the bed map folded under a service charter that promises excellence for every line. "No one loses in this draft," a chief says. Marco points to Thursday’s bed crunch. "Then who waits when orthopedics gets the block?" The group has to choose before the board packet goes out.
examples.whatToDo: Make the bed conflict explicit, choose the service line that gets priority this quarter, and state who waits instead of hiding the cost.
examples.whyItMatters: A plan designed to offend nobody cannot allocate scarce beds. The queue turns politeness into a visible tradeoff.

examples.title: Yusuf Tests the Broadest Grant
examples.scenario: After last year’s cancellations, Yusuf no longer trusts the grant score sheets by themselves. He spreads them beside a rehearsal calendar and donor pledges in the arts board office. The broadest proposal predicts the highest score again: youth access, innovation, community, touring, and training. Yusuf has to decide whether to reward breadth or test which plan survives the cash gap before opening night.
examples.whatToDo: Compare the score sheets with canceled rehearsals, then favor the plan that solves cash timing instead of the one with the broadest language.
examples.whyItMatters: Ambiguity wins scoring rounds because it sounds generous. The rehearsal calendar shows which promise can actually reach the stage.

examples.title: Grace Reorders the Offsite Around Dependencies
examples.scenario: Why does every team still have a top priority after the ranking exercise? Before lunch, Grace watches product, platform, security, and sales place team priority cards in the keep column. After she lays the dependency board beside the release date, she stops the offsite. Before anyone votes again, she changes the sequence: pick the blocking dependency, name the team that waits, then rebuild the priority list.
examples.whatToDo: Start with the dependency board and release date, then make every team priority answer that constraint before it stays in the plan.
examples.whyItMatters: The old ranking protected every group. The new sequence makes agreement depend on a real exclusion.

questions.prompt: A committee approves a plan quickly because every department sees its favorite project included. No budget increase is available. What should you infer?
choices: Fast agreement may mean the plan avoided the exclusion that budget limits require.
Fast agreement proves the plan is aligned and ready for execution.
Fast agreement means the group should add more detail later but keep the portfolio intact.
questions.explanation: The budget cap means inclusion has a cost. Quick agreement can be a warning that no department has yet been asked to lose.

questions.prompt: A city task force writes “safe, vibrant, inclusive streets” into its plan. Crash records show one dangerous intersection creates most injuries. What is the most strategic next move?
choices: Keep the phrase because it reflects shared values across the city.
Name the intersection as the constraint and decide which other street projects wait.
Launch a broad public art campaign so residents feel ownership.
questions.explanation: The crash records create a precise choice. Shared values and art may help later, but ambiguity should not hide the intersection tradeoff.

questions.prompt: A family business retreat protects every owner’s pet project because nobody wants a fight. A failing assembly step is causing returns. What does the retreat reward?
choices: Technical precision in diagnosing returns.
A healthy culture of inclusion that should remain untouched.
Ambiguity that preserves relationships while delaying the needed tradeoff.
questions.explanation: The retreat rewards peace over choice. Inclusion becomes costly when it keeps resources from the assembly failure driving returns.

questions.prompt: A university committee loves the phrase “distinctive pathways,” but enrollment data show two tracks compete for the same faculty. What question should break the fog?
choices: Which track gets protected this year, and which one is paused or merged?
Can the phrase be made more inspiring for prospective students?
Should the committee schedule another listening session before data review?
questions.explanation: The faculty constraint requires a track choice. Better language or more listening can postpone the decision without resolving the conflict.

questions.prompt: A hospital plan wins approval because every service line is praised equally. Bed data show one service must get priority to reduce waits. What is wrong with the approval?
choices: The plan is too optimistic about patient demand.
The approval is shallow if it avoids saying which service absorbs the bed tradeoff.
The plan should have used more clinical evidence in the introduction.
questions.explanation: Equal praise hides the scarce-bed decision. The issue is not tone or evidence volume; it is avoided allocation.

questions.prompt: An arts board gives high scores to proposals that mention access, innovation, community, and experimentation. Canceled productions show cash timing is the recurring failure. What should change?
choices: Reward proposals that directly solve the cash-timing problem, even if their language is narrower.
Keep rewarding breadth because more values means more public benefit.
Ask applicants to add stronger community language to every budget.
questions.explanation: The scoring system rewards ambiguity. The canceled productions show the constraint that should govern funding decisions.

questions.prompt: A software offsite ends with all teams keeping their top priorities, even though one dependency blocks the release. What does this reveal?
choices: The teams collaborated well because nobody left empty-handed.
The release date should be moved before dependencies are discussed.
The offsite avoided the political cost of naming which team waits.
questions.explanation: Keeping every priority protects groups from loss. The dependency requires a choice about who waits, which the offsite avoided.

questions.prompt: A director says vague language is necessary because the organization needs unity. When is that unity counterfeit?
choices: When people agree before any real constraint or exclusion has been named.
When the plan includes values that cannot be measured immediately.
When the plan takes longer than one meeting to approve.
questions.explanation: Unity becomes counterfeit when agreement depends on leaving the cost unnamed. Values can be useful, and approval time is not the real issue.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit avoids choosing between legal aid and rent relief by calling both “housing stability pillars.” Funding covers only one pilot. What should a strategist do?
choices: Run both pilots at half strength to keep the coalition together.
Ask which pilot answers the most urgent obstacle and state why the other waits.
Rename the pillars so donors see them as complementary.
questions.explanation: The funding limit makes a choice unavoidable. Half-strength pilots and renaming preserve ambiguity instead of deciding what the obstacle requires.

reviewCards.front: A room agrees quickly before any tradeoff is named. What should you suspect?
reviewCards.back: Suspect cheap consensus. Agreement may be real, but it is shallow until the constraint and the losing priority are named.

reviewCards.front: Why does ambiguity feel useful inside institutions?
reviewCards.back: It protects coalitions, lowers political cost, and lets different groups hear their own priorities in the same language.

reviewCards.front: What turns broad consensus into strategy?
reviewCards.back: The group must name the constraint, accept the tradeoff, and decide which priority waits. Agreement after that point is more meaningful.

reviewCards.front: A plan praises every service equally while resources are scarce. What question retrieves the move?
reviewCards.back: Ask who gets priority and who waits. Scarce resources turn politeness into evasion unless the plan states the allocation.

reviewCards.front: How can you challenge ambiguity without becoming cynical?
reviewCards.back: Treat ambiguity as a social incentive, not a character flaw. Ask what cost the language avoids and what decision would make the plan real.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice reading consensus for the tradeoff it may be hiding. The skill is to honor the need for cooperation while still naming the constraint, the loser, and the political cost.

ifThenPlans.plan: If everyone agrees before a constraint is named, then ask what choice would make one group unhappy and put that choice on the table.
If a budget plan includes every priority, then mark the cap in plain numbers and ask which priority waits.
If the language gets broader as disagreement rises, then translate one broad phrase into a specific allocation decision.
If a coalition avoids choosing among real needs, then name the people affected by delay and choose the first tractable intervention.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, revisit one easy agreement and write the exclusion it avoided. Share the exclusion as a question, not an accusation.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one meeting note for consensus language. Beside each broad phrase, write the constraint it should decide or mark it as unresolved.

memorableLines.text: Consensus becomes expensive the moment it meets a constraint.
Counterfeit consensus needs fog.
Ambiguity is attractive because it feels humane.

chapters.title: The Kernel of Good Strategy
chapters.hook: Three linked sentences can do more strategic work than a hundred approved initiatives.
chapters.counterintuition: The kernel can look tidy and still fail if its three parts drift apart. Diagnosis, policy, and action have to test one another as a chain.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one sentence for diagnosis, one for guiding policy, and one for action. If the third sentence could fit a different diagnosis, rewrite it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use the kernel as a chain: diagnose the obstacle, choose the governing response, then align actions tightly enough to test whether the response works.

breakdown.fastRead:
Hannah places the missed-visit log beside a bus route sheet and an exam-room schedule. The clinic has been blaming patients for no-shows. The route sheet tells a different story: the last bus arrives after the first morning appointments. Hannah crosses out reminder texts and a waiting-room poster. The diagnosis is access timing. The guiding policy is to make appointments fit the bus reality. The coherent action is a new morning block and fewer stranded slots.

The chain holds only when the diagnosis, policy, and actions stay connected. Break the chain and the plan becomes a phrase, a slogan, or a task list.
breakdown.deepRead:
Etienne stands over a dealer map for a marine equipment distributor entering a new province. A shipping crate with a damaged pump sits by the door. The margin table shows that small dealers can sell the product but cannot handle returns. Etienne asks whether the company is solving awareness or service coverage. The answer changes everything.

Diagnosis names the obstacle before action earns trust. Guiding policy chooses the kind of response. Coherent action makes that response real. The kernel works only when diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action stay connected as one chain.

Those parts sound simple because each one is plain. Their power comes from the connection. If the diagnosis is weak, the guiding policy floats. If the policy becomes vague, action scatters. If action does not match the policy, the diagnosis becomes an essay no one can use. The kernel is compact, but it is not soft. Each part tests the others.

Frida sees the failure in reverse after a vocational college misses apprenticeship targets. The placement roster shows that students are qualified. Employer calls show supervisors need one reliable contact before taking another apprentice. The workshop schedule is full of resume sessions, which look helpful but do not answer the employer obstacle. In the postmortem, the kernel becomes clear: employer confusion, single-contact policy, and a placement desk that owns every callback.

A good kernel makes action narrower and stronger at the same time.
breakdown.fullRead:
Luca hears the phrase “mid-market analytics” for the fifth time and stops the sales meeting. On the table are a sales call transcript, a segment list, and trial data. The transcript shows finance teams asking the same question about monthly close errors. The segment list says retail, logistics, SaaS, and healthcare all look promising. The trial data says finance teams activate fastest. Luca marks finance close errors as the obstacle and asks which segment will wait.

That is what the middle part of the kernel does. A diagnosis by itself can be true and still leave too many doors open. A guiding policy closes some doors by naming the response pattern that will govern choices. For Luca, the policy is not “sell analytics better.” It is “win finance teams with close-error detection before broadening.” That policy is useful because it can reject work.

You can test your own plan the same way. Does the diagnosis explain why current effort fails? Does the guiding policy tell you what kind of action belongs? Do the actions make the policy visible in budgets, schedules, owners, and stopping rules? If the answer is no at any step, the kernel has a loose link.
